issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a trauma context dominated by interpersonal assault or ambush cues (others' sudden movements, ominous silence) rather than toxic chemical exposure. For a chemical exposure trauma, these are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported assault/combat context.

issues.item: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal about losing connection to community/culture is not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The other selected items center on intrusive memory, overwhelm, and coping incapacity, but there are no related triggers, memories, or strategies suggesting social/cultural disconnection as a core post-trauma theme.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: This item is the least coherent with the rest of the profile. For a 72-year-old married male Coast Guard patient with toxic chemical exposure, the dominant pattern elsewhere is threat, intrusive sensory memory, and low coping around reminders. 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is not impossible, but it is not well supported by the trauma type or by the other selected threat/memory/appraisal items, which center on danger, overwhelm, and inability to handle recall. It reads as a broader social-identity consequence that is disconnected from the active formulation, where Memory and Threat are tightly linked and Negative Appraisals are threat-focused. This makes that individual appraisal item clinically weakly matched to the rest of the self-report.

vignette: Elias Vance stood on the dock where the Coast Guard cutter had first pulled alongside the ruptured cargo ship, the yellow mist still clinging to the metal railings in his mind. He had been twenty-four when the tanks cracked, when his captain ordered the crew to seal the hatch without proper gear, and when the air turned acrid against his skin. That day, his body had reacted with violent, unyielding physical force: his breath catching in his chest, his stomach turning, his hands trembling until he could no longer grip his equipment. Thirty years later, those reactions still arrived unannounced. A passing truck backfiring, the hiss of a pressure washer, the sharp tang of industrial cleaner in a hardware aisle, and his pulse would spike, his palms would sweat, and his muscles would lock into a rigid brace. He told himself nothing was wrong with his lungs, yet his body continued to respond to the atmosphere itself. Over the years, the memory did not fade; it simply learned how to live in his head. Elias found the images returning with photographic clarity, snapping into place like a developed print he could not put away: the cracked drum heads, his own soot-stained knuckles, the way the vapor had curled over the deck grating. When the memory returned, he felt so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing, set down his tools or his coffee cup, and step away until the weight lifted. He was certain that if he let the memory play, it would not stop. It replayed over and over in the quiet corners of his day, looping the same thirty seconds until his chest grew tight. He had come to believe that if he thought about the event, he would not be able to handle it, so he kept his mind on the weather, on the crossword, on the rhythmic sweep of the windshield wiper. He changed the channel the moment he heard the word drum. He avoided documentaries about chemical plants. He did not look back. The world outside had shifted in his perception. He was certain that the world is dangerous, that safety was a temporary pause rather than a guarantee. His home, which should have been a place of rest, became a perimeter he had to constantly map. He checked the deadbolts twice, listened for the wind against the siding, and kept his chair facing the entryway when he sat in the living room. Unusual silence left him on guard even inside his own home. When the television was off and his wife turned a page in her book, his stomach tightened, convinced that something dangerous was about to happen. He had learned to fill the quiet with the radio, with the hum of the kitchen fan, with a steady stream of practical talk, because the stillness felt like a held breath waiting to break. These habits had shaped his routine in ways he could no longer ignore. At the old Coast Guard station where he had spent twenty-eight years, he used to know every creak of the dock and every sound a cutter made when it pulled into the slip. Now, when he walked past the marina on his morning route, the low murmur of an idling engine made his breathing turn shallow. He stopped attending the veterans’ gathering because the quiet waiting room made his chest ache, and he no longer stayed long when his wife asked him to look over a repair manual in the garage. The enclosed space felt too tight, and the smell of old paint and cleaning solvents brought the yellow mist back so sharply that he had to step outside, leaving the book on the workbench. His hands, once steady enough to calibrate navigation equipment, now shook when he reached for a wrench. He could not deal with even the slightest upset; a dropped key, a misaligned calendar, a sudden draft made him feel unmoored, as if his body no longer trusted his own mind to keep him steady. What finally brought him to the clinic was the quiet at his own table. One evening, his wife reached for his hand while the radio played softly in the background, and the sudden silence between her words made him flinch so hard he knocked his glass over. He stood up, his breath catching, certain that the floor would tilt and the walls would close in. He walked out to the driveway and sat on the hood of his truck until his pulse slowed, terrified that he was losing control of everything he had spent decades holding together. He had come to believe that the world is dangerous, that he was no longer equipped to navigate it, and that the memories would keep playing until he simply ran out of breath. He was seeking help not because he wanted to forget, but because he wanted to sit at his kitchen table without bracing for impact, because he hoped to hear a silence without waiting for the other shoe to drop, and because he wanted to stop feeling like a stranger in his own life.
